objective: The Triangle Emerges. Here's the aha moment: when you line up all those ring-rectangles by their radius (shortest at bottom, longest at top), they form a triangle! The base is the outer circumference 2πR, the height is R. Triangle area = ½ × base × height = ½ × 2πR × R = πR². That's where the formula comes from

finalists.title: Reshape Triangle to Match Error Annotation
finalists.narrative_wrapper: The student sees a triangle with incorrect proportions (wrong base-to-height ratio) labeled with a miscalculated area that doesn't equal πR². An error indicator shows 'Off by: X%' and points to where the triangle shape is wrong. The student grabs the triangle's edges or corners and reshapes it directly—stretching the base wider or pulling the height taller—and the system continuously calculates backward to determine which ring-rectangle correspondence would produce that triangle shape, displaying those rings in a circle diagram alongside.
finalists.manipulated_variable: The student directly manipulates the triangle's base length or height by dragging the triangle's edges, which inversely determines and displays which rings (at which radii) must be included in the stack to geometrically produce that triangle profile; the system solves backward from desired triangle shape to required ring selection.
finalists.primary_visual_feedback: As the student stretches the triangle's base or adjusts its height, the adjacent circle diagram dynamically updates to show which rings would need to exist (some rings appear, disappear, or change thickness) to create that exact triangle when stacked. A color gradient flows from each ring in the circle to its corresponding horizontal layer in the triangle. The error percentage shrinks as the shape approaches the correct 2πR base and R height ratio.
finalists.goal_structure: Concrete target: reshape the triangle until the error indicator reads '0%' and all rings in the circle diagram have consistent thickness (indicating a real circle of radius R). The student commits by releasing the drag, then sees the correct formula derivation overlay appear.
finalists.causal_chain_exposed: Live readouts show the current base measurement, current height, the implied outer radius R_implied (base/2π), the ratio height/R_implied (should equal 1.0 for consistency), and the resulting area calculation ½ × base × height. A consistency meter shows whether the triangle shape could actually come from a real circle or represents an impossible geometry.
finalists.trace_strategy: Previous incorrect triangle attempts leave faint ghost outlines that fade over 3-4 seconds, showing the path of exploration. Each ghost is annotated with its error percentage. This creates a visual history of the search process, revealing how different base/height ratios lead to physically impossible ring configurations (rings of inconsistent radii).
finalists.aha_moment: By manipulating the final triangle shape and watching the system solve backward for which rings could produce it, the student discovers that only ONE specific triangle shape (base=2πR, height=R) corresponds to a consistent set of rings all from the same circle—any other triangle proportions require rings from circles of different sizes, revealing why the formula must be exactly πR² and not some other expression.
finalists.feasibility_sketch: Requires custom SVG/canvas code for dynamic triangle manipulation and live feedback updates.
finalists.weakness: The complexity of backward-solving for ring configurations may confuse students without clear initial guidance.

finalists.title: Drag Rectangles to Stack into Triangle
finalists.narrative_wrapper: The student sees concentric rings from a circle, each cut and unrolled into a rectangle of different length. They drag these rectangles from their scattered starting positions and stack them vertically in order by length. As they align them, a triangular silhouette emerges.
finalists.manipulated_variable: Individual rectangle position via dragging, changing the vertical arrangement order from scattered to sorted by radius
finalists.primary_visual_feedback: The rectangle being dragged moves with the cursor, and snap guides or alignment hints appear when near the correct stacking position; adjacent rectangles may highlight or shift slightly to show insertion point
finalists.goal_structure: Concrete target: all rectangles must be placed in ascending order by length with their left edges aligned, forming a complete stacked triangle shape
finalists.causal_chain_exposed: Each rectangle displays its corresponding radius value and circumference length as labels; the emerging triangle shows live calculation of base (2πR) and height (R) measurements that update as rectangles snap into place
finalists.trace_strategy: Correctly placed rectangles remain fixed in position as persistent visual elements; a triangle outline progressively appears/completes as more rectangles are correctly stacked, showing the accumulating geometric relationship
finalists.aha_moment: The circle's area formula emerges visually when the stacked variable-width rectangles suddenly resolve into a recognizable triangle whose dimensions directly connect to the circle's radius and circumference
finalists.feasibility_sketch: Requires custom SVG/canvas code for draggable rectangles and dynamic alignment feedback.
finalists.weakness: The design relies heavily on the learner's ability to spatially organize and align rectangles, which may be challenging without clear initial guidance.

narrative_draft.text:
We've sliced the circle into rings and unrolled each one into a thin rectangle. We've even stacked them all together. But here's the strange part: the pile doesn't *look* like anything familiar yet. How do we get from a wobbly stack of rectangles to the clean formula πR²?

The answer is hiding in how you arrange them. Right now, the triangle in front of you is slightly off—its base is too short, or maybe its height is stretched wrong. The error indicator shows exactly how far the area calculation misses the mark. Grab the triangle's corners and reshape it, stretching the base wider or pulling the height taller. As you adjust the shape, watch what happens to the rings shown in the circle beside it: they shimmer in and out, thicken and thin, as the system figures out backward which rings from which circle would actually stack up to form your triangle. Most triangle shapes you try will demand rings from circles of completely different sizes—a geometric impossibility if we're working with just one circle.

Keep reshaping until the error vanishes. You'll find there's only one triangle that works: base exactly 2πR (the outer circumference), height exactly R (the radius). Any other proportions break the ring-to-layer correspondence. When the shape locks into place, the area formula appears not as a rule to memorize but as the only possibility: ½ × base × height becomes ½ × 2πR × R, which simplifies to πR². The formula isn't handed down from above—it's the inevitable consequence of geometry keeping its promises.
